column1: Why can't sibling components in Angular directly bind properties or send events to each other?
column2: Angular has no sibling-to-sibling binding mechanism. Data flows strictly down via @Input() and up via @Output() to their shared direct parent, which acts as the switchboard.

column1: What is the correct way for a deeply nested grandchild component to pass an event up to a grandparent component?
column2: The grandchild emits an @Output() event to its direct parent. The parent's template catches it and explicitly re-emits its own @Output() event up to the grandparent (one hop at a time).

column1: Why does ngOnInit() fail to update a component when a parent modifies an @Input() property later in the application lifecycle?
column2: ngOnInit() is a one-time lifecycle hook that runs only once after the initial input setup. It does not re-run when @Input() values change later.

column1: When should you choose an @Input() setter instead of implementing ngOnChanges()?
column2: Use an @Input() setter when you need simple, self-contained logic that reacts to changes in a single input, without needing access to previous values or other input properties.

column1: Why must a parent component pass a new object reference (e.g., { ...this.settings, maxLength: 200 }) when updating an @Input() object?
column2: Angular compares object inputs by reference. Mutating an object's properties in place does not change its memory reference, so Angular's change detection and ngOnChanges will not detect the change.

column1: What rule must be followed when defining an @Input() setter in TypeScript?
column2: You must define both a set and a matching get property. Without a getter, TypeScript will prevent the property from being read inside the class or template.

column1: What is the risk of using an untyped EventEmitter() (or EventEmitter<any>)?
column2: It removes TypeScript's type safety net, allowing type mismatches between the payload emitted by the child and the argument expected by the parent's handler to pass without compile errors.

column1: Why should child components extract DOM values before emitting (e.g., (e.target as HTMLTextAreaElement).value)?
column2: Extracting the value inside the child ensures it emits clean domain data (like a string), keeping DOM-specific implementation details contained within the child component.

column1: What is the guaranteed execution order of component lifecycle events in Angular?
column2:
1. Constructor
2. ngOnChanges() (first run)
3. ngOnInit()
4. ngOnChanges() (on subsequent input updates)
5. ngOnDestroy() (before removal)

column1: Why should setup logic that depends on @Input() properties be placed in ngOnInit() instead of the constructor()?
column2: The class constructor() runs during plain TypeScript object instantiation before Angular has assigned @Input() values. ngOnInit() is guaranteed to run after initial inputs are set.

column1: What is the primary benefit of adding TypeScript interfaces like implements OnInit, OnDestroy to a component class?
column2: They provide compile-time type checking. If you misspell a hook name (e.g., ngOnDestory), TypeScript will throw a compilation error rather than letting the method silently fail at runtime.

column1: What object parameter does the ngOnChanges() lifecycle hook receive?
column2: It receives a SimpleChanges object containing key-value pairs for only the @Input() properties that changed during that specific change-detection cycle.

column1: In ngOnChanges(changes: SimpleChanges), how do you retrieve the value of an input named text prior to the update?
column2:
Use changes['text'].previousValue.

Note: this.text already holds the new value by the time ngOnChanges executes.

column1: What does changes['text'].firstChange evaluate to on the very first call to ngOnChanges()?
column2: It evaluates to true. On all subsequent calls for that input property, it evaluates to false.

column1: Why is key-guarding (e.g., if (changes['text'])) essential inside ngOnChanges() for components with multiple inputs?
column2: ngOnChanges() fires whenever any input changes. Key-guarding ensures logic specific to one property only runs when that specific property actually changed in that cycle.

column1: In a scenario where a parent clears text to '', why must a stats panel child component use ngOnChanges() to reset its counts?
column2: Because ngOnInit() only runs once upon creation. Only ngOnChanges() runs on subsequent input updates to recalculate and reset displayed counts live.

column1: Under what condition will ngOnChanges() NOT fire for a component?
column2: It will not fire if the component has no @Input() properties, or if none of its bound @Input() properties changed during the change-detection pass.

column1: When exactly does the ngOnDestroy() lifecycle hook execute?
column2: It executes exactly once, synchronously, immediately before Angular removes the component instance from the DOM and detaches it from change detection.

column1: Why do background timers like setInterval() cause memory leaks if not cleaned up in ngOnDestroy()?
column2: The browser keeps references to running timers alive even after the component's DOM node is removed, executing callbacks on an unrendered component instance.

column1: Which types of event listeners require manual cleanup in ngOnDestroy() versus template bindings like (click)="..."?
column2: Listeners manually attached to global objects (e.g., window.addEventListener) require manual cleanup. Template bindings managed by Angular are cleaned up automatically.

column1: How do you safely clean up a setTimeout reference inside ngOnDestroy()?
column2: Store the timer handle in a property (e.g., private timerId?: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout>) and execute clearTimeout(this.timerId) inside ngOnDestroy().

column1: What primary role does Zone.js play in Angular's default change-detection system?
column2: Zone.js patches asynchronous browser APIs (DOM events, timers, Promises) to notify Angular whenever an async task completes, triggering a change-detection pass.

column1: What happens across the component tree during a default Angular change-detection pass?
column2: Angular traverses every component top-to-bottom, re-evaluates template expressions, updates changed DOM nodes, and calls ngOnChanges() for children with updated @Input()s.

column1: Does updating a class property inside a standard (input) or (click) handler require manual change detection triggers?
column2: No. Standard template event handlers are patched by Zone.js, which automatically triggers a change-detection pass right after the handler function completes.

column1: What is the fundamental difference between Change Detection and the ngOnChanges() lifecycle hook?
column2:
Change Detection is Angular's overall tree-walking mechanism to update the DOM.

ngOnChanges() is just one lifecycle hook called during that process when input values change.

column1: Why should state be held in a common parent component in a multi-component hierarchy?
column2: Holding shared state in the parent maintains a single source of truth and keeps data flow traceable, since siblings cannot communicate directly.

column1: When a settings component allows editing nested settings, how should it emit updates to preserve immutability?
column2: It should emit a completely new object (e.g., this.settingsChanged.emit({ ...this.settings, maxLength: newLimit })) rather than mutating existing properties.

column1: How does [maxlength]="limitEnabled ? maxLength : null" affect the native HTML textarea element?
column2: When limitEnabled is true, it sets the native maxlength attribute to the number value. When false (null), Angular completely removes the attribute from the DOM element.

column1: How does *ngIf="false" differ from CSS display: none regarding component lifecycles?
column2:
*ngIf="false": Completely destroys the component and triggers ngOnDestroy().

CSS display: none: Keeps the component mounted in the DOM and active in change detection.

column1: Why is reference replacement required for non-primitive inputs when preparing for OnPush change detection?
column2: Reference-based checks only evaluate memory addresses. If the reference address doesn't change, Angular assumes the data is identical and skips view re-rendering.
